cases.title: Sensitive Care Segregation vs. Clinical Records
cases.statement: California requires segregating and geo-restricting medical information 'related to' abortion, gender affirming care and contraception. Relatedness in a clinical record is a matter of inference, not a field.
cases.analysis: § 56.101(c)(1) demands four capabilities: restricted access, no out-of-state disclosure, segregation from the rest of the record, and automatic disablement for out-of-state users. Misoprostol and methotrexate have other indications. An hCG lab, an ultrasound, a pharmacy refill, a problem-list entry or a free-text note can each be related or unrelated depending on context. A tagger has false negatives, which leak protected data out of state. It also has false positives, which hide clinically needed data from out-of-state treating clinicians. Federal information-blocking rules mostly defer to state law through the 'required by law' clause, so the hard part is classification.
cases.inclusionReasoning: No classifier can decide 'related to' with certainty from the record, and both error directions cause legal or clinical harm. Exclusions in (c)(4) narrow who is covered but not the classification problem.

cases.title: EDR Anonymity vs. Crash Trace
cases.statement: The EU General Safety Regulation requires event data recorders that capture precise pre-crash data and can't be deactivated. It also requires that data to be 'anonymised' and unable to identify the vehicle.
cases.analysis: Art. 6(4)(a) requires speed, braking, position and safety-system activation at high accuracy. Art. 6(4)(c)(iii) requires the data to identify type, variant and version. Art. 6(5) forbids storing anything 'which could allow the individual vehicle itself, its owner or holder, to be identified'. The EDR sits in a specific car that is towed, inspected and linked to a police report. A precise crash trace from a known wreck identifies the driver. Recital 13 limits the claim to 'the stored data' alone, but that reading conflicts with recital 14 and with how EDR data is read in practice.

cases.title: DMA 6(7) Wi-Fi interoperability vs. single-account trust domain
cases.statement: Apple must let third-party connected devices auto-join the user's Wi-Fi networks. Today it shares saved Wi-Fi passwords only with devices on the same Apple Account.
cases.analysis: The specification decision lists the shared data: SSID, BSSID and the network password. Apple's trust boundary for that secret is the Apple Account. A third-party watch has its own vendor account and its own vendor cloud. Para 107 says integrity under the DMA "does not allow gatekeepers to impose their own model of security and privacy". So Apple can't require the device to join its account, and must release a credential to a device whose trust root it doesn't control. Every new vendor is a new root that holds the user's network password.

Per-device consent prompts don't restore it, since the secret still leaves the domain. Only a level-down (shrinking Apple's own feature) changes the equation, and that drops the property for first-party devices.

cases.statement: Organizers that encrypt users' messages, or let users encrypt them, must give the FSB the information needed to decode them. The same article requires messengers to keep messages confidential.

A service can meet 4.1 only by holding keys, and holding keys makes every message readable by the organizer and anyone who compromises it.
cases.inclusionReasoning: Endpoint-held keys and a duty to supply decoding information can't both hold. Any mechanism that lets the organizer supply keys makes the organizer able to decrypt. Distinct from N12: a standing statutory duty with no notice or review step.

cases.title: CERT-In VPN subscriber records vs. no-log VPN
cases.statement: India's 2022 CERT-In Directions make consumer VPN providers register validated subscriber identities and the IPs each member used, and keep them five years. A no-log VPN keeps no record linking a user to an IP or session.
cases.analysis: Para (v) requires validated names, addresses, hire periods and "IPs allotted to / being used by the members", held for 5 years after the account closes. Para (iv) adds 180 days of ICT system logs. FAQ Q34 limits (v) to providers of Internet proxy-like services to the general public, which is the consumer VPN market. A no-log, anonymous-signup VPN is built so the operator can't answer who used an exit IP at a given time. Records of validated identity plus allotted IPs are the answer to that question. A provider can't hold the records and also lack them. The FAQ's offshore-storage allowance in Q35 changes where the records sit. They still exist.
cases.inclusionReasoning: No. Shared-exit, no-log designs can't produce member-to-IP records, and keeping them removes the property. Passes on the same footing as the other Deliberate Blindness cases, where one mandate conflicts with a security property and no opposing law is needed. ExpressVPN removed its Indian servers on 2 June 2022, per its own notice. Other removals are press-reported.

cases.title: China game real-name registration vs. threshold-only age proof
cases.statement: China requires every online game user, adult or minor, to register and log in with real identity information checked through the NPPA verification system. A threshold-only age proof tells the operator one fact: whether the user is over 18.
cases.analysis: The rule being enforced needs one bit per user. Minors may play 20:00 to 21:00 on Fridays, weekends and public holidays, and the notice sets no limit for adults. Item 2 of the 2021 NPPA notice fixes the method: every game connects to the NPPA real-name verification system, every user registers with "真实有效身份信息" (real and valid identity information), and guest mode is banned. Order 766 Art. 46 repeats the verification duty in a State Council regulation. So an adult who only needs to show adulthood must still register a real identity. An anonymous age credential isn't identity information, and the operator can't serve a user on it. PIPL Art. 6 limits collection to the minimum scope the purpose needs. Art. 13(1)(3) allows processing needed to meet a statutory obligation, so the real-name rule prevails. The mandate names identity as the input, so a threshold-only token can't stand in for it.
cases.inclusionReasoning: No. A threshold-only proof would be enough to apply the time limits, but item 2 requires real identity registration through the NPPA system and bans service to anyone without it. An operator can't comply and also learn only one bit. Spending doesn't change what the notice names as the input. The national network ID hides the plaintext ID from the platform and still hands it an identifier tied to one person.

properties.name: Unlinkability
properties.note: The operator learns whether the user is over 18 and nothing else, and no party can link the proof to a person. Item 2 requires real identity registration for every user and bans service without it.

shapes.name: Verification vs. Minimization
shapes.rationale: Verification-minimization: the time-limit rule needs one bit about each user, and the mandated check collects identity from all of them. The mandate fixes the method, so a minimal proof isn't an accepted substitute. Drafted by claude-fable-5-1. cases.title: Russia unified app store mandate vs. single-root iOS distribution
cases.statement: Since 1 September 2025 Russian consumer law bars any condition on smartphones and tablets that restricts installing apps through the unified app store, or the functions, updates and payments of those apps. iOS installs only code the platform vendor has reviewed and signed.
cases.analysis: Art. 4(4.1) puts a unified app store among the programs that listed devices must carry pre-installed. Government Decree No. 1867 lists smartphones and tablets. Art. 4(4.2), added by 194-FZ, removes the platform's controls over that store. No condition may restrict installing programs through it, restrict search, updates, settings or notifications for its apps, set special pricing terms, or limit payment methods. 194-FZ also amended the preamble, so a device that fails 4.1 or 4.2 is a defective good under the law. The iOS security model has one root: the vendor reviews and signs everything that runs. A second store that installs and updates code on its own decision is a second root. A vendor review or signing step that can refuse one of that store's apps is a condition restricting installation, which sub-item 1 bars. The three sub-items carry no exception for security or integrity measures.
cases.inclusionReasoning: No. Single-root distribution means one party decides what installs. Art. 4(4.2)(1) bars any condition that restricts installation through the unified store, so the vendor can't keep its review as a gate. Notarization, capability limits and payment rules are each a restriction the sub-items name. Spending doesn't help, because the conflict is over who holds the root. A vendor keeps the property only on devices that aren't sold in Russia.

properties.name: Single Trust Root
properties.note: Only code reviewed and signed by the platform vendor installs and runs on the device. Art. 4(4.2)(1)-(2) bars conditions that restrict installing, updating or running apps from the unified store.

shapes.name: Trust-Root Monopoly vs. Plurality
shapes.rationale: Trust-root-plurality: the platform's property is one review and signing root, and the statute requires a second store to install and update code free of the platform's conditions. Drafted by claude-fable-5-1. Signed off by Will Foti without domain review, 2026-11-06, on claude-fable-5-1's source verification.
